Cannabis 101

Will CBD Show Up on a Drug Test? Why THC Is the Real Issue

Standard tests look for a THC breakdown product, not CBD. Here is why a CBD product can still lead to a positive result, and how to lower the odds.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20268 min read

08min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. Will CBD show up on a drug test? How screening works
  2. CBD types and how much THC each can contain
  3. How your body handles CBD, and whether it turns into THC
  4. Can CBD cause a failed drug test?
  5. CBD oils and gummies
  6. Urine, blood, saliva and hair tests compared
  7. Lowering your risk
  8. When to talk with your employer or a clinician
  9. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Standard workplace tests look for a breakdown product of THC, not for CBD.
  • The risk comes from THC in the product: full spectrum contains some by design, and mislabeled products can contain more than they say.
  • In a Johns Hopkins study published in 2025, CBD oil with as little as 0.5 mg of THC per dose led to positive urine tests during twice-daily use.
  • A 2017 review found no sign that swallowed CBD turns into THC in people.
  • No CBD product can promise a clean test. If you are tested, check your employer's policy and talk with a clinician first.

Will CBD show up on a drug test? Standard drug tests don't look for CBD at all. They look for a breakdown product of THC, the compound in cannabis that causes a high. The catch is that many CBD products contain some THC, by design or by mistake, and that THC can be enough to turn a test positive. Here's how testing works, where the risk comes from and how to lower it.

Will CBD show up on a drug test? How screening works

Urine is the most common sample in drug testing. The first step is a screening test, called an immunoassay, that looks for THC-COOH, a compound your body makes as it breaks down THC. As of 2026, federal workplace programs count a screen as positive at 50 nanograms per milliliter. A positive screen then goes to a second, more precise lab test, which counts the sample as positive at 15 nanograms per milliliter or more.

CBD isn't part of that standard panel. So the real question isn't whether a test can find CBD. It's whether your CBD product put enough THC into your body to cross those cutoffs.

CBD types and how much THC each can contain

The three main types of CBD carry different amounts of THC:

TypeTHC contentDrug-test risk
Full spectrumContains THC by design; hemp's legal limit is 0.3% THC, not zeroHighest
Broad spectrumProcessed to remove THC to levels a lab can't detectLower, but labels can be wrong
IsolateMore than 95% CBDLowest, though not zero

A small percentage can still add up. For example, 0.3% of a one-gram serving of oil is 3 milligrams of THC, and some people take more than one serving a day. Our guide to full-spectrum CBD explains why those products keep their THC.

Labels aren't always right, either. A study published in 2024 tested CBD products bought online in late 2021. Roughly one in three that named a type on the package didn't meet that type's definition, and three products sold as broad spectrum contained THC.

How your body handles CBD, and whether it turns into THC

A common worry is that stomach acid turns CBD into THC. That idea comes from lab experiments using simulated stomach fluid. A 2017 review concluded that those conditions don't match a real stomach, and that the conversion hasn't been seen in people, even after high doses of CBD by mouth. People given CBD in controlled clinical trials also haven't shown THC's typical side effects, such as feeling high.

That fits what you may already know: CBD doesn't intoxicate the way THC does. Our article asking whether CBD is psychoactive covers that question. A 2026 review still lists conversion, during manufacturing or in the body, as a possible risk, so the question isn't completely closed. For drug testing, though, the clearer risk is THC that came along with the CBD.

Can CBD cause a failed drug test?

A 2026 review of studies on CBD and hemp oils traced positive results mainly to what's in the product. The sample tested, how the product was taken and how sensitive the test was also played a part. In practice, that points to four routes:

  • THC by design. Full-spectrum products contain THC, and daily use adds up.
  • Mislabeling. A product can hold more THC than its label says, or THC it claims not to have.
  • Contamination. THC can find its way into a product during manufacturing, even when it isn't meant to be there.
  • Secondhand smoke. This rarely matters at workplace cutoffs. Federal guidance notes positives only under extreme exposure, such as riding in a closed car with people smoking, and only at a screening cutoff below the workplace standard.

A Johns Hopkins study published in 2025 shows how little THC it can take. Healthy adults took CBD oil with between 0 and 3.7 mg of THC per dose. In the first eight-hour session, at least one person in each group taking 1 mg of THC or more tested positive. During two weeks of twice-daily use, every group whose oil held any THC produced positives, even at 0.5 mg. One sample from the group with no added THC tested positive too, and two positives turned up a week after people stopped.

The researchers noted that standard tests can't reliably tell legal hemp products from other cannabis use, and that a positive can follow doses too small to cause a high.

CBD oils and gummies

Oils and tinctures make it easy to adjust a dose, which also makes it easy to take more than you planned. With a full-spectrum oil, every extra dropper adds THC along with the CBD. In the Johns Hopkins study, which used CBD oil, the number of positive samples rose with the THC in each dose.

Gummies feel more predictable, since each piece is pre-measured. Still, a gummy carries whatever THC is in the extract inside it, and a daily gummy habit is the kind of repeated use that let positives build up in that study. Read the THC line on a gummy's label as closely as you'd read it on a bottle of oil.

Urine, blood, saliva and hair tests compared

The main types of drug tests cover different stretches of time. A 2012 SAMHSA guide for clinicians gives these broad estimates for THC:

TestWhat it picks upTypical window
UrineTHC-COOH, THC's main breakdown productUp to about 3 days after a single use, up to about 10 days with heavy use and 30 to 36 days with chronic heavy use
BloodRecent useShort, since most drugs leave the blood quickly
SalivaRecent use, largely THC left in the mouthGenerally the previous 24 to 48 hours
HairUse over a longer stretchAbout 3 months is typical, but not the most recent 7 to 10 days; light use is hard to detect

These windows move with how much and how often you use, your body and the cutoff a lab chooses. They describe THC, since that's what these tests are built to find.

Lowering your risk

No CBD product can promise a clean test. If you're subject to testing, the only way to remove the risk entirely is to skip CBD products. If you use them anyway, these steps lower the odds:

  • Choose isolate over full spectrum. It carries the least THC.
  • Read the THC figure, not the front of the package. Look at THC per serving and per package.
  • Look for batch testing. Licensed Michigan products list their testing lab and test date. For CBD bought elsewhere, a lab report should match your product's batch number and include THC.
  • Be skeptical of big promises. Words like THC-free and drug-test safe are marketing, and testing has caught products that didn't live up to their labels.
  • Use less, less often. Repeated daily doses are what let positives build up in the two-week study.

Our guide to reading a cannabis label shows where each number sits on a Michigan package.

When to talk with your employer or a clinician

If your job, license or sport involves testing, ask your employer or program what its policy says about CBD before you start. Ask, too, how it handles a positive result from a legal product, since a test can't tell where the THC came from.

Talk with your doctor or pharmacist as well. They can look at your other medicines and your health history and help you decide whether CBD makes sense for you.

Our budtenders can explain any product label, but no one can predict a test result. Find your nearest store on our locations page. Our stores serve adults 21 and older, and medical patients 18 and older with a card. Use cannabis responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

Can CBD isolate cause a failed test?

It's possible, though less likely than with other types. Standard tests look for a THC breakdown product, and isolate is more than 95% CBD. The risk comes from THC that shouldn't be there. Product testing has found items that didn't match their labels, and one study recorded a positive sample even in a group taking CBD oil with no added THC.

How long does CBD stay in your system?

For a standard drug test, the CBD itself doesn't matter, because the test looks for THC's breakdown product. What matters is how long any THC from your product lingers. SAMHSA's urine estimates for cannabis run from up to about three days after a single use to 30 to 36 days with chronic heavy use. In one study of CBD oil with small amounts of THC, positives still appeared a week after people stopped.

Do drug tests check for CBD?

Standard workplace tests don't. They screen urine for THC-COOH, a breakdown product of THC, at a 50 ng/mL cutoff, then recheck positive screens with a more precise test at 15 ng/mL. CBD isn't part of that usual panel. The concern with CBD products is the THC that some of them contain, whether it's listed on the label or not.

Is dispensary CBD different from convenience-store CBD?

The labels are. Licensed Michigan dispensary products are tested and labeled with their THC and CBD content, the testing lab and the test date. CBD from other shops may not show the same details, and studies of CBD products sold online have found many that didn't match their labels. Some dispensary products pair CBD with THC on purpose, so read both numbers.

Sources

  1. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration: Clinical Drug Testing in Primary Care, Technical Assistance Publication 32 (2012)govinfo.gov
  2. Wolinsky D. et al., The acute and chronic pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of oral cannabidiol with and without low doses of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, Journal of Analytical Toxicology (2026 issue; published online July 2025)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  3. Ovat D.Y. et al., Impact of CBD and hemp oil use on drug test results: a systematic review, International Journal of Legal Medicine (2026)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  4. Gidal B.E. et al., Product labeling accuracy and contamination analysis of commercially available cannabidiol product samples, Frontiers in Pharmacology (2024)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  5. Nahler G. et al., A conversion of oral cannabidiol to delta9-tetrahydrocannabinol seems not to occur in humans, Cannabis and Cannabinoid Research (2017)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  6. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Marihuana Rules, R 420.1 to R 420.1004 (packaging and labeling)michigan.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
